newsitem.title: USA: Health officials study anti-AIDS drug and childhood cancer.
newsitem.headline: Health officials study anti-AIDS drug and childhood cancer.

text.p: The drug AZT remains the best way to prevent an AIDS-infected pregnant woman from passing the virus onto her unborn child, despite some mice studies that suggest a possible risk of eventual cancer in the children, medical experts said Tuesday.
The panel of experts convened by the National Institutes of Health said more research is needed into the possible AZT cancer link and that children exposed to it in utero should be carefully tracked.

And pregnant women considering AZT, or Zidovudine, treatment to avoid perinatal transmission should be informed of the possible risks, the experts agreed at the end of a full-day of meetings reviewing the research. A formal statement finalizing their conclusions will be completed in the next few days.
So far, there have been no cases of cancer in children linked to AZT, although since the drug has only been used widely for a few years it could be too early to detect a problem.
The Center for Women Policy Studies issued a statement late Tuesday demanding the federal government reverse its guidelines recommending the routine use of AZT.

"It is time to reverse course in light of this new study and the fact that AZT is no longer the standard of care for anyone living with HIV or AIDS," the group said. "It would be a travesty to ignore these disturbing new findings."

The U.S. Public Health Service has recommended AZT therapy for pregnant women infected with the HIV virus that causes AIDS since 1994 and "those recommendations are good, solid recommendations for treatments," said Dr. John Killen, director of the AIDS division at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases at NIH.
AZT was the first drug introduced to fight AIDS, and although it did not prove effective on its own against the HIV virus, it was shown to cut the risk of transmission to the baby by two-thirds.
There is a 23 percent change of passing the virus onto the unborn child without AZT, and the risk drops to under 8 percent with AZT.
AZT is now used in combination with new drugs to suppress the AIDS virus, and studies are underway to see how those drug "cocktails" affect maternal transmission.
The panel, drawing on experts from around the country, reviewed two studies, both on mice. In one of those studies, the lab animals had been given "relatively highish doses" of AZT.

The Center for Women Policy Studies said federal health officials had rushed to recommend the routine use of AZT on the basis of one clinical trial "without knowing the long-term effects of AZT on pregnant women and their fetuses."
